Every time an order changes state, Kestrel sends a POST request to the endpoint you registered. The body is a JSON event, and the request is signed, so you can be sure it came from us and not from someone who found your URL.

How it works

Webhooks are the fastest way to follow a parcel without polling. Setting one up takes three steps:

  1. Register an HTTPS endpoint under Developers, Webhooks and choose the events you want.
  2. Copy the signing secret that appears once, and store it next to your other secrets.
  3. Answer every request with a 2xx status within five seconds. Do the slow work afterwards.

Verify the signature

Each request carries three headers. The one that matters is Kestrel-Signature: a timestamp and an HMAC-SHA256 of the timestamp and the body, signed with your secret.

Header What it carries
Kestrel-Signature The timestamp and signature, as t=…,v1=….
Kestrel-Event The event type, for example order.paid.
Kestrel-Delivery A unique id for this attempt. Log it, support will ask for it.

Use the raw body

Compute the signature over the bytes you received, before any JSON parser touches them. Re-serialising the body changes whitespace and key order, and the signature will never match.

Frameworks that parse JSON for you usually keep the raw body on the request object. Find that property once, and verify from it.

Replay protection

Reject any request whose timestamp is more than five minutes old. A stolen request is then useless to whoever replays it, and you do not have to store anything to know.

Retries and ordering

If your endpoint answers with anything but a 2xx, or does not answer in time, we retry with growing gaps: one minute, ten minutes, one hour, then every six hours for two days. Events are not guaranteed to arrive in order, so compare the updated_at field before you overwrite anything.

  • Make your handler idempotent: the same delivery can arrive twice.
  • Store the delivery id, and skip ones you have seen.
  • Return 410 to stop retries for an endpoint you have removed.

Test it locally

The CLI forwards live events to a port on your machine and prints the signing secret for that session, so you can develop without a public URL. 

          {"kestrel listen --forward-to localhost:3000/webhooks"}
